articles.title: Kate Winslet gave £17,000 to a mother facing soaring bills for her daughter’s life-support equipment; a year later, the mother launched a fundraiser to help other families with energy costs
articles.summary: A mother whose daughter depends on life-support equipment around the clock has started a national fundraising campaign to help other families struggling
articles.body: A mother whose daughter depends on life-support equipment around the clock has started a national fundraising campaign to help other families struggling with high energy bills. The move comes a year after Hollywood actress Kate Winslet stepped in to pay off her own rising energy costs. Carolynne Hunter, a 50-year-old project lead for the charity Pamis who lives in Stirlingshire, Scotland, faced annual electricity bills of up to £17,000 to keep her 13-year-old daughter Freya alive. Freya has severe and complex health needs. She is non-verbal and blind, and depends on a constant oxygen supply and nursing care at home around the clock. Local council officials warned that running the medical equipment Freya needs, along with heating their home in Tillicoultry, would cause their energy bills to rise sharply. In response, Ms Hunter launched an online fundraising appeal in late 2022. Oscar-winning actress Kate Winslet donated £17,000 directly to the campaign after following Ms Hunter's public efforts to highlight the pressures faced by unpaid carers. After receiving the donation, Ms Hunter confirmed that she no longer had to worry about paying her immediate heating and electricity bills. She then joined forces with GoFundMe to launch a new campaign to help other families across Scotland who care for children with life-shortening conditions.Campaign for social tariffs and charitable supportMoney raised through Ms Hunter's new GoFundMe campaign is being directed to Children's Hospices Across Scotland. The organisation provides care at home, hospital support teams and hospice services for babies, children and young people up to the age of 21. Speaking to the Press Association news agency, Ms Hunter explained how the original donation came about and why she decided to keep campaigning for other families. “Kate saw me campaigning the governments and wanted to donate to me to help with my energy bills, so GoFundMe contacted me and helped me set up a GoFundMe page so she could,” Ms Hunter told the Press Association. “This then went viral and many more kind people donated too.” Ms Hunter said the celebrity donation gave her family greater financial security, but thousands of other carers still lack reliable support. “I worked with GoFundMe to set up a fundraiser to support families this Christmas who are in a similar situation to me last year to hopefully raise money to help them with their bills, but whilst doing that, it can also give me a platform again to start talking a bit more widely about what the UK Government had promised last year in terms of a social tariff,” she said. Social tariffs are discounted rates for essential household services, such as gas, electricity and broadband. They are designed to help low-income households and people whose medical needs require large amounts of electricity.Medical challenges and emotional toll on carersThe physical and emotional demands of providing intensive medical care at home became especially difficult shortly after the donation. In December 2022, both Ms Hunter and Freya became ill with winter illnesses. Freya was admitted to hospital with severe flu, while Ms Hunter was treated for pneumonia. Freya remained in hospital until February 2023. Speaking to the Press Association about that period, Ms Hunter explained that keeping the house warm was important for their recovery, but the experience also placed a lasting strain on her. “When you're looking after a child like Freya, it's just complete intensive care constantly, you don't get a break,” Ms Hunter told the Press Association. “As much as I have support to look after Freya, she is ultimately my responsibility and I am on call constantly.” Ms Hunter also revealed that she had recently been diagnosed with complex post-traumatic stress disorder. She believes the condition is common among family carers who provide full-time care and deal with medical emergencies without enough wider support. “I have recently been diagnosed with complex Post-traumatic stress disorder and that will be common among other families, that is just the way it is,” she said.Government responses and policy debateMs Hunter has criticised both the Scottish and UK governments for failing to introduce special electricity rates for households that need to run energy-intensive medical equipment at home. “The Scottish and UK governments have not provided adequate support for families with a high level of medical need,” she told the Press Association. “They have promised social tariffs and health board support at meetings and FMQs. However, it has still not delivered to families.” In response to the campaign, government representatives pointed to financial support schemes already available to vulnerable households. A spokesperson for the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said the government had spent £40 billion helping to cover household energy bills across the UK during periods of sharp price rises in winter. “We're also continuing to support the most vulnerable, with three million households expected to benefit from the £150 Warm Home Discount, £900 for those on means-tested benefits, and an extra £150 for disabled people,” the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson said in an official statement. In Scotland, Energy Minister Gillian Martin expressed sympathy for the Hunter family and highlighted welfare schemes run by the Scottish Government to support disabled children. “No parent should ever have to worry about how they will afford essential care for their children, and I would like to express my sympathies to Carolynne Hunter and her family,” Martin said in a statement released by the Scottish Government. Martin pointed to the Scottish Government's £30 million Fuel Insecurity Fund, along with targeted payments such as the Child Winter Heating Payment and Child Disability Payment. She said these were among the main measures used to help vulnerable families manage rising living costs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 29-year-old self-described professional gambler allegedly ran a $10 million Ponzi scheme targeting over 400 investors; FBI offers $150,000 reward
articles.summary: A 29-year-old man accused of running a Ponzi scheme that allegedly defrauded more than 400 investors has been added to the FBI’s Most Wanted Fraudsters
articles.body: A 29-year-old man accused of running a Ponzi scheme that allegedly defrauded more than 400 investors has been added to the FBI’s Most Wanted Fraudsters list. Imer Gomez is accused of raising approximately $10 million by promising investors high returns from stock market trading. According to the FBI, the funds were allegedly used to finance a lavish lifestyle and pay earlier investors, while clients received fake account statements showing fictitious gains. Gomez was charged with wire fraud after a federal grand jury indictment in July 2025. The SEC separately accused him of defrauding clients of approximately $9 million.How the alleged $10 million Ponzi scheme targeted more than 400 investorsAccording to the SEC’s complaint, Gomez began soliciting prospective clients in August 2021, offering investment advisory services through K&G Investment Solutions LLC. He later used Helios Venture Fund LLC, a company he controlled, to solicit further investments. The SEC described Gomez as a self-identified professional gambler with no known experience investing or managing money on behalf of clients.The SEC alleged that Gomez presented himself as an experienced securities trader who could generate monthly double-digit returns by trading securities for clients. He also allegedly told prospective investors that their accounts were insured for up to 75 per cent of their value in certain circumstances. The complaint stated that Gomez obtained approximately $9 million in client deposits during the period from August 2021 to September 2023.The SEC alleged that neither K&G nor Helios operated as an investment fund, despite the latter company’s name. Instead, the companies were presented as investment advisers that would manage individual client portfolios. Under the agreements signed by investors, the companies claimed they would actively trade selected exchange-traded funds and individual stocks on clients’ behalf.Fake account statements in the alleged $10 million Ponzi schemeThe SEC’s complaint alleged that the promised investment services were never provided. According to the regulator, Gomez and the companies did not use clients’ money to trade securities, create individual investment accounts or obtain the insurance coverage they had promised. Instead, funds were allegedly placed in bank accounts controlled by Gomez and mixed together.To persuade investors that their money was growing, Gomez allegedly sent them account statements showing increasing balances and fictitious gains. The SEC said these statements did not identify actual transactions and instead listed values that Gomez had artificially increased. According to the complaint, some investors were persuaded by the statements to send additional money for investment.The SEC alleged that the money was used for personal expenses, unrelated business ventures and payments to earlier investors. The regulator said Gomez used the majority of the approximately $9 million received from clients for these purposes, as well as for payments to third parties, employees, referral commissions and cash withdrawals. No client funds were transferred to a trading platform.SEC alleges $666,000 went to Gomez’s associatesThe SEC also alleged that Gomez transferred approximately $666,000 in commingled client funds to Eric Claxton and Heather Claxton. Eric Claxton was identified in the complaint as the father of Gomez’s former girlfriend. The SEC said the money was received between 2022 and 2023, with some payments described as loans.According to the complaint, Eric Claxton initially deposited $100,000 with Helios in March and April 2022 and received that money back by June 2022. He subsequently received approximately $196,000 from Helios and Gomez between June 2022 and March 2023, while the couple jointly received a further approximately $370,000 between June and August 2023. The SEC alleged that these payments came from commingled client funds and that the Claxtons had not repaid amounts purportedly loaned to them or provided services or other value in exchange.The SEC’s complaint also described how Gomez allegedly attempted to reassure investors after the money ran out. In a letter sent on September 19, 2023, Gomez said Helios had been affected by a “sudden and unrecoverable liquidation”. He did not identify the reasons for the alleged event, citing a strict non-disclosure agreement. The SEC alleged that the supposed liquidation was actually the point at which Gomez ran out of money from new clients to continue the scheme.FBI investigates Gomez on wire fraud chargeThe FBI said Gomez was indicted by a federal grand jury in the US District Court for the Western District of Texas on July 16, 2025, and that the indictment had recently been unsealed. The agency said he was believed to be avoiding prosecution in Mexico. The FBI’s October 2026 announcement concerns the criminal wire fraud charge, while the SEC’s earlier case involved alleged violations of federal securities laws.The SEC filed its civil complaint on July 14, 2025, in the US District Court for the Western District of Texas. It accused Gomez and Helios of violating provisions of the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The regulator sought permanent injunctions, the return of alleged ill-gotten gains with interest, and a civil penalty against Gomez. It also sought the return of funds received by Eric and Heather Claxton.FBI offers $150,000 reward for information on GomezThe FBI said its Most Wanted Fraudsters list was launched in June 2026 to encourage public assistance in locating fugitives wanted in major fraud cases. The agency announced that a reward of up to $150,000 was available for information leading to the arrest and conviction of a person on the list.Anyone with information about Gomez’s case is urged to contact the FBI’s toll-free tipline. The FBI said individuals' information may remain anonymous. The allegations in the SEC complaint and the FBI’s announcement concern separate legal proceedings. The SEC’s claims are allegations set out in a civil complaint, while the FBI’s announcement states that Gomez has been charged with wire fraud. The allegations should not be presented as a finding of guilt.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: John Oliver’s show bought nearly $15 million in medical debt for $60,000 in 2016; instead of collecting it from around 9,000 people, it worked with a charity to wipe their outstanding bills
articles.summary: In June 2016, television comedy host John Oliver bought nearly $15 million (£11.8 million) in unpaid medical debt for just $60,000 (£47,000) through a
articles.body: In June 2016, television comedy host John Oliver bought nearly $15 million (£11.8 million) in unpaid medical debt for just $60,000 (£47,000) through a debt collection company created for the purpose. Instead of using debt collectors to demand payment from the roughly 9,000 patients linked to the accounts, the producers of HBO's Last Week Tonight with John Oliver transferred the entire debt portfolio to a specialist charity to have it wiped out. The television segment showed how the little-known American market for buying and selling unpaid debt works. In this market, third-party collection agencies buy unpaid consumer and medical bills for a small part of their original value.Setting up a collection agency for $50To carry out the debt giveaway, the production team behind Last Week Tonight registered a debt collection company called CARP (Central Asset Recovery Professionals) Inc. in Mississippi. It paid just $50 (£39) to set up the company. Although the newly formed company had no previous experience in finance or debt collection, it passed basic regulatory checks without difficulty. This allowed the producers to buy a group of overdue medical bills from hospitals in Texas. The bills had a total face value of $14,922,261.76 (£11.7 million), but CARP Inc. bought them for a single payment of $60,000. Under normal collection practices, debt agencies try to recover money from individual borrowers through letters, phone calls and warnings about possible damage to their credit records. These companies can still make large profits even if they recover only a small share of the total debt they purchase. Oliver took a different approach. During the broadcast, he pressed a red button on stage to officially transfer the entire group of debts to RIP Medical Debt, a nonprofit organisation now known as Undue Medical Debt.Partnering with a specialized charityUndue Medical Debt was founded in 2014 by Craig Antico and Jerry Ashton. Both were former executives in the debt collection industry who used their knowledge of the market to help people get relief from medical debt. After Oliver's production company transferred the accounts, the charity sent letters to the 9,000 people affected. The letters told them that their medical debts had been cleared completely, with no tax liability attached. According to statements published by Undue Medical Debt, the television broadcast brought the charity national attention and showed how donations could be used to remove the financial burden of medical bills. A donation of $1 can help erase about $100 in medical debt at its original value. The charity selects debt portfolios linked to people earning less than twice the federal poverty line or facing serious financial hardship. Health policy analysts writing in The British Medical Journal noted that the stunt exposed a wider problem in the United States healthcare system. Unexpected medical emergencies can leave uninsured or underinsured patients facing long-term financial hardship and debt they cannot repay.A landmark television momentDuring the broadcast, Oliver explained that buying medical debt was legally simple and surprisingly cheap, given the serious financial problems these bills can cause for families. “As it stands, debt buying is a scummy business, and it needs much stricter oversight,” Oliver said during the episode. “Because as it stands, any idiot can get into it. And I can prove that to you, because I’m an idiot, and I started a debt-buying company.” Oliver said the giveaway broke the previous record for the largest financial giveaway in American television history. That record had been held by Oprah Winfrey, who famously gave new cars worth about $7.9 million (£6.2 million) to her studio audience in 2004. “We are forgiving $15 million in medical debt,” Oliver told viewers as he triggered the transfer. “It seems clear that medical debt collection is bad, and we need to fix it.” After the episode aired, the production team shut down CARP Inc. and handed all its records to Undue Medical Debt. This ensured that no one could try to collect payment on the accounts in the future.Broader institutional initiativesThe approach shown on Last Week Tonight has since been used by local governments and groups that buy healthcare services to help reduce medical debt across communities. An official press release from Undue Medical Debt explained how the nonprofit worked with the Campaign to End Medical Debt and the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions to expand regional debt relief projects across the United States. Through these partnerships, local government grants and private donations are used to buy medical debt directly from hospitals and companies that trade in unpaid accounts. Recent updates from the organisation show that state and county governments, including authorities in New Jersey, Kentucky and Arizona, as well as Cook County, Illinois, have committed public money to erase billions of dollars in medical debt for lower-income residents. These efforts use the same debt-buying methods highlighted in Oliver's 2016 broadcast.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: French newspaper rips Macron after riots erupt across France: ‘Indelible stain’
articles.summary: The scathing critique in newspaper Le Figaro took aim at Macron, France’s justice system and immigration policies after nationwide protests erupted into violence.
articles.body: A prominent French newspaper delivered a blistering critique of the country’s leadership after nationwide protests descended into riots, looting and arson. The article, written by Vincent Trémolet de Villers for the conservative newspaper Le Figaro and published Sunday afternoon local time, blamed years of political failures for contributing to the unrest and took particular aim at President Emmanuel Macron. It criticized what it described as a justice system that is "lenient toward criminals," accused far-left groups of carrying out violence with little consequence and took aim at France’s immigration and security policies. "A judiciary that is lenient toward criminals but unrelenting toward decent citizens. The incomprehensible privilege of these far-left militias, who destroy, set fires, and kill with impunity," the article stated, according to a translation. "An uncontrolled immigration, in which a portion of the immigrants rebels against the country that took them in." WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED The article also took aim at Macron over his past calls for police to show greater empathy. "Emmanuel Macron’s reprimands toward a police force he deemed insufficiently 'empathetic' — directed at officers under attack by bolts, cobblestones, and mortar fireworks — will remain an indelible stain," it stated. The author argued that the unrest reflected deeper failures by France’s political establishment. "If the far-left, criminals, and looters can turn France upside down in a matter of hours, it is primarily because a technocratic monarchy — intoxicated by its own self-importance — has methodically dismantled all the moral, security, cultural, and economic safeguards that allow a society to remain standing." The scathing assessment followed a day of violence across France, where masked groups clashed with police, looted businesses, set fires and attacked public buildings, according to The Associated Press. Macron addressed the nation Sunday, condemning the violence and vowing that those responsible would be held accountable. PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE "Nothing will excuse their actions. We all tonight feel angry. We feel shame as well," Macron said, according to a translation of his televised remarks. "There needs to be a response. Those people who looted need to pay for their crimes," he added. The French president also acknowledged concerns raised by the youth about their economic prospects and futures. "The youth of our nation are expressing great anguish and concern about the future, the conditions of where their careers will take them, what role they will be able to play in society," Macron said. "… I hear what they are saying, for the past ten years I've been fighting for them, so we need to pay heed to what they are saying." Macron said he ordered officials to increase security around public buildings and businesses, with protests potentially restricted in some areas. At least 2,400 people were arrested nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region, according to the AP. More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, the AP reported, citing Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Hundreds of businesses were looted nationwide, and unrest continued Sunday in Paris, where police used tear gas as tensions flared around Place de la République. The criticism also comes as Macron faces scrutiny over his decision to attend a Celine Dion concert with his wife, Brigitte, on Friday night, on the eve of the nationwide demonstrations. The protests, fueled in part by anger over rising living costs, school conditions and public services, erupted into violence Saturday. Macron's office and Le Figaro could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment. Fox News Digital's Bradford Betz and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: House prices are on the rise - how does your area compare?
articles.summary: Affordability continues to be a "real challenge" for buyers, as prices rise by an average of 4%.
articles.body:
Affordability continues to be a "real challenge" for some house buyers, after prices in Wales rose by 4% in the year to June.

The market has shown "real resilience" with prices more than 7.5 times the average income in some areas, according to new figures from the Principality Building Society (PBS).

Anglesey topped the chart with a 22% annual rise, but 17 of Wales' 22 local authority areas saw price increases, the Wales House Price Index said.

Ceredigion was one of four regions to see a price drop and Aberystwyth estate agent Layla Mangan, said she has noticed "a lack of confidence" amongst buyers and sellers who were feeling "uncertain" about cost of living pressures.

The overall average house price was £258,129, but Andy Mottram of PBS said, while the market had shown "real resilience" with "strong price growth" in many places, "affordability was a real challenge for people".

Flintshire, saw no annual change and, of the four local authority areas to see a decline, Ceredigion had the the biggest drop of 9% - although Mangan said that did not reflect her experience in Aberystwyth.

First-time buyers were facing average house prices equivalent to four-and-a-half times household income in Cardiff, compared with just over three-and-a-half times in Blaenau Gwent where houses were cheapest, according to the data.

For people who were already home owners and wishing to move, purchase prices were equivalent to 7.6 times income in Cardiff and 5.2 times in Blaenau Gwent.

Blaenau Gwent saw a 47% increase in the number of mortgages issued between April and June compared to the first three months of 2026, the biggest increase in Wales.

First time buyer properties in the area cost an average of £155,000 with an overall house price of £167,239.

But Blaenau Gwent also had the lowest average household pre-tax income at £42,000 according to the report.

This contrasts with Monmouthshire which had the highest household income at £61,700 as well as the most expensive average house prices at £285,000 for a first-time buyer and £387,606 overall.

Layla Mangan from Alexanders estate agent in Aberystwyth said she was "surprised" at the 9.3% drop in prices recorded for Ceredigion.

"That's not been our experience" she said, "it's a hard market, yes, but it doesn't feel that we've dropped nearly 10%".

But Mangan said she has noticed "a lack of confidence" among buyers and sellers.

"We don't have to look hard to work out why that would be. What an uncertain time we're in," she said.

"I can understand people feel reluctant to wanting to essentially get into more debt. I understand that and it's hard at the moment."

"Everybody is really into house prices, whether you're a homeowner or not, because we can use it as this kind of thermometer, this gauge for what the economy and our finances are doing in general," she said.

"If you aren't looking at selling again in 12 months' time I'd hold your nerve, I'd go for it.

"We can't expect to be buying houses and making money on them straight away and where we go wrong is if that's what we're expecting."

The number of houses sold in a region can impact how much prices rise or fall compared to other places.

On Anglesey, which saw the biggest annual rise in house prices of 22.2%, the market can be a mixed picture.

Richard Tuke has lived on the island for 20 years but now wants to sell up and live in Spain.

"Anglesey has always been a desirable area for people to live," he said, adding he thinks the market is "not as bad as it was".

After several months of little interest he has twice reduced his asking price, from the initial £475,000 to £425,000, and that has made a difference.

"We've had a wave of viewings in the last two weeks and a lot of strong interest, so I think we're at the right price level now," he said.

The turbulence in the Middle East and the knock-on effects on oil and gas prices have already led to higher rates for fixed rate mortgage deals, and the Bank of England is widely expected to increase interest rates, making borrowing more expensive in the months ahead.

"If you look back over the year to date, the market's shown remarkable resilience in spite of those pressures," said Mottram.

"I think that's broadly likely to continue as we look forward."

Mottram said that despite building cost of living pressures, there were a variety of options for would-be home buyers.

"There's still going to be pressures," he said, but "if people are worried, the best thing they can do is talk to their lender or talk to a mortgage broker to understand their options".

articles.title: Priest killed by falling crucifix during livestreamed Mass as worshippers rush to help
articles.summary: Video captures the moment a large wooden crucifix fell on Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari during a livestreamed Mass in Guayaquil, Ecuador.
articles.body: A priest preparing Communion was fatally struck by a falling crucifix during a livestreamed Mass in Ecuador, turning a moment of worship into a frantic rush to save him. Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari was standing at the altar of Nuestra Señora del Perpetuo Socorro Church in Guayaquil on Saturday when the large wooden crucifix behind him suddenly fell forward and struck him. Video of the service captures screams erupting inside the church as worshippers ran to his side and called for help. HISTORIC NYC CHURCH ENGULFED IN 5-ALARM BLAZE; 6 FIREFIGHTERS INJURED BATTLING STUBBORN FLAMES The Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his death in a Facebook statement, identifying him as the parish priest of Perpetuo Socorro Church in its Central Vicariate. "Our dear Fr. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari … has departed to the Father’s House to enjoy His presence and His glory," the archdiocese wrote in Spanish. "Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord. And let perpetual light shine upon him. May he rest in peace. Amen," the statement concluded in Latin. The tragedy unfolded just one day after the archdiocese congratulated Sánchez Molinari on the anniversary of his ordination, Ecuadorian news outlet Primicias reported. MASKED MAN CAUGHT ON CAMERA SMASHING VIRGIN MARY STATUE WITH A HAMMER OUTSIDE NYC CHURCH The Mass was being livestreamed on social media when the crucifix fell, recording both the fatal incident and the desperate response from those inside the church. "Father, Father … call an ambulance," a woman can be heard shouting in the video. Sánchez Molinari belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, commonly known as the Redemptorists. Before serving in Guayaquil, he spent several years as parish priest at San Lorenzo in Vinces, in Ecuador’s Los Ríos province, according to Primicias. articles.summary: A property-line disagreement in St.
articles.body: A property-line disagreement in St. Charles County, Missouri, turned into a criminal case after police said a neighbour fired a gun toward a man repairing a fence. Paula Kohensky, 60, has been charged with first-degree assault or attempted assault and armed criminal action following the Sunday-night incident. According to court documents cited by First Alert 4, the alleged shooting happened while the man was using an electric grinder to cut a misaligned fence post.The neighbour’s wife told police that someone had shot at her husband, prompting an investigation. Kohensky initially did not come out of her home to speak with officers, but eventually did so about 30 minutes later. She is being held on a $500,000 bond and is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on December 2, according to court records.What police say happenedThe man told investigators that he had been working on the fence through Sunday evening after a property-line dispute involving him, Kohensky and her husband. He said he brought out an electric grinder to cut a fence post that had been misaligned. According to the probable cause statement, he heard yelling while the grinder was running, followed by a countdown from three and then a gunshot. He ran back inside and asked his wife to call police, as per the report.Kohensky later told police that she had a history of harassment and stalking issues involving the neighbours. She said she decided to walk her dog in the backyard that night and left the house carrying a handgun, it was further reported.The neighbour’s account and the videoKohensky told police she heard loud metal scraping and saw sparks coming from beneath a tarp covering the fence. She said she saw her neighbour’s shadow, yelled at him to get away from the fence and claimed the gun accidentally went off while she was holding it, reported First Alert 4 and Hawaii News Now.Police said surveillance video from the neighbours’ home told a different story. The footage allegedly showed Kohensky and her husband standing side by side while Kohensky pointed a gun at the fence. According to the court documents, the gun appeared to fire before Kohensky’s husband took it from her. The two then went back inside their home.The charges and what comes nextReports suggest that Kohensky faces two felony charges: first-degree assault or attempted assault and armed criminal action. The charges stem from the alleged shooting during an ongoing neighbourhood dispute, according to court documents. She is currently held on a $500,000 bond. Her preliminary hearing is scheduled for December 2, according to court records cited by First Alert 4.At this stage, the allegations remain accusations. A preliminary hearing will help determine whether there is enough evidence for the case to proceed, and any final determination of guilt would come through the court process.Why fence disputes can escalateProperty-line disagreements are among the most common sources of neighbour conflict. A fence sits directly at the boundary between two homes, making questions of ownership, maintenance, placement and access highly personal.In this case, police said the dispute had already involved multiple people and a history of alleged harassment and stalking. That context matters because ongoing conflict can make ordinary repairs feel threatening, even when the work itself is routine.The incident is also a reminder of how quickly disputes can become dangerous when firearms are involved. A disagreement over a fence post, a boundary line or a repair job should be handled through communication, documentation, mediation or legal channels rather than confrontation.A case still unfoldingThe alleged shooting has left a neighbourhood dealing with the aftermath of a dispute that escalated far beyond a property boundary. Police say the evidence includes both the neighbour’s account and surveillance footage, while Kohensky’s defence may address her claim that the gun discharged accidentally.For now, the case remains pending. The court will examine the charges, the video evidence and the circumstances surrounding the alleged shooting before determining how the matter proceeds.You use AI every day. articles.title: Donald Trump announces Tom Fazio-designed redevelopment of 106-year-old East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, plans 15-month closure despite court order halting tree removal
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has announced plans to close Washington, DC’s historic East Potomac Golf Links from November 15 for a 15-month redevelopment,
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has announced plans to close Washington, DC’s historic East Potomac Golf Links from November 15 for a 15-month redevelopment, despite an ongoing legal challenge over his administration’s plans to transform the public course into a world-class golfing destination.In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump said the Department of the Interior, under Secretary Doug Burgum, had developed the redevelopment plan in collaboration with renowned golf course architect Tom Fazio. The President said the redesigned course would remain open to the public while meeting the standards required to host major international tournaments.The announcement comes amid a legal battle over the project. A federal judge last week ordered a halt to the redevelopment until at least October 26 after criticising the administration for beginning extensive tree removal at the site over a holiday weekend without adequate notice to the court or the plaintiffs challenging the makeover.Trump did not address the court proceedings in his post, which also included an artist’s rendering of the proposed redesign.Trump announces redevelopment plan with architect Tom FazioAnnouncing the proposal, Trump said the Department of the Interior had worked with Fazio to develop a plan for a championship golf course at East Potomac Golf Links, a 106-year-old public facility near the White House.“I am pleased to announce that the Department of the Interior, under the auspices of Secretary Doug Burgum, and in conjunction with famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio, has developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote.He said the redesigned course would be accessible to the public while being capable of hosting some of the sport’s biggest tournaments, including the US Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup.“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” he added.Trump also said the United States Golf Association, PGA of America and PGA Tour had been notified about the proposed course and would have it on their list of venues for major events.Trump cites jobs and economic benefits of golf course makeoverIn his post, Trump argued that the redevelopment would generate employment and bring economic benefits to Washington, DC, and surrounding areas.“This Course will create many Jobs, and have a tremendously positive Economic Development impact on Washington, D.C., and the surrounding area. Millions of Dollars will inure to the Capital area,” he wrote.The President, who regularly plays golf, has made the proposed makeover part of a broader effort to renovate prominent sites in the US capital. Other projects associated with his administration include plans for a large ballroom at the White House, changes at the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and the construction of a massive arch. Several of these initiatives have faced legal challenges.East Potomac Golf Links has long been a public facility accessible to Washington residents across income groups. Opponents of Trump’s redevelopment plans have argued that turning it into a high-end golfing destination could change its character and make it less affordable for ordinary golfers.Trump calls existing course unsafe, defends tree removalTrump described the existing course as being in poor condition and said its infrastructure required major restoration.“The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall,” he wrote.He also defended the removal of hundreds of trees at the site, saying the course had originally been known for having few trees and offering unobstructed views of Washington, DC.“When the East Potomac Course was originally built, it was famous for no trees, with views of Washington, D.C., for all to see, but now, it is completely overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe,” Trump said.According to his announcement, restoration work based on Fazio’s design will begin on November 15, when the existing course will close to golfers. Trump said the new course would open in approximately 15 months.The tree removal has become a central issue in the legal dispute. US District Judge Ana Reyes ordered a halt to the work after an emergency hearing, criticising the administration for failing to provide sufficient notice to the court and the plaintiffs before the trees were cut down, according to AP.The controversy has also drawn attention to debris from the demolition of the White House East Wing, which was cleared to make way for Trump’s planned ballroom. The National Park Service has said the debris tested positive for lead, chromium and other toxic metals. The material was also reported to have been dumped on the golf course grounds.Federal judge to examine Trump’s golf course plansThe announcement could complicate a federal court hearing scheduled for Monday in a lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League and two golfers seeking to stop the redevelopment.Judge Reyes has ordered key members of the administration to testify about the recent tree-cutting operation and whether it was connected to Trump’s plans for the historic public course.During an emergency hearing on October 12, Reyes expressed frustration with the administration’s handling of the tree removal, questioning why the court and the plaintiffs had not been properly notified before the work began.The administration subsequently asked for Reyes to be removed from the case, challenging her impartiality and describing her conduct during the hearing as “egregious”. The judge is expected to address that request at the upcoming proceedings.Meanwhile, the plaintiffs have asked the court to impose a longer-term preliminary injunction or a stay to prevent the redevelopment from proceeding while the legal challenge is considered.You use AI every day. articles.title: Alberta independence referendum: Will separatists survive a loss?
articles.summary: Alberta’s independence movement faces likely defeat, but history suggests losing a referendum may not end the fight.
articles.body:
Cory Morgan has spent more than 25 years fighting for Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta to become an independent country. On Monday, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the issue for the very first time. But even if the answer is no, Morgan said he’s in it for the long haul.

“I would respect the will of the voters,” he told Al Jazeera. “If they’ve decided it’s not time to go that route yet, then so be it. But that doesn’t mean I’ll stop.”

Morgan, the founder of the advocacy organisation Pathway to Independence, is among a group of longtime separatists who have managed to push what was once a fringe idea onto the ballot.

Monday’s provincial referendum asks Alberta residents to weigh whether they would like to pursue a binding resolution in the future on the question of independence.

Polls indicate the pro-independence side has little chance of succeeding, with four of five people in the province saying they want Alberta to remain a part of Canada. But Morgan’s focus is on the one in five who don’t.

“That’s not a movement that’s leaving,” he said.

What the referendum will mean for the separatist movement and for Canada as a whole, however, is a more complicated question.

Monday’s ballot gives Albertans two options: to remain part of Canada or begin the legal process for holding a future referendum on separation.

A vote in favour of the second option doesn’t mean Alberta immediately becomes an independent country.

Any province that tries to secede would first have to go through complex negotiations with the federal government in Ottawa, other provinces and Indigenous peoples who live in and around Alberta.

Some separatist organisers have been using that distinction to encourage people to vote for the referendum — even if they don’t necessarily want independence.

“Strategic separatists and their leaders have been using that ambiguity, that lower-bar threshold, to entice folks to vote not to leave, but rather to send Ottawa a message that Albertans need to be heard,” said Jared Wesley, a political science professor at the University of Alberta.

He told Al Jazeera that the message may be resonating with some voters.

Data collected by Viewpoint Alberta, a University of Alberta-based research initiative, suggests that two-thirds of voters who support the referendum say they’re doing so for strategic reasons, to send a message to Ottawa.

These are people Morgan calls “reluctant separatists”, people who are “at the end of their rope” and simply want Ottawa to pay attention.

But Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned Albertans against this strategy.

“Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” he told a pro-Canada rally in Calgary on Thursday. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.”

What’s driving Alberta’s separatist movement?

Monday’s referendum has been decades in the making. Separatists have long felt that Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, sends too much money to Ottawa, subsidising the rest of the country while receiving little in return.

They also take issue with federal energy policies that they feel limit the potential of the province’s oil industry.

For Morgan, the resentment stretches back to the 1980s when the National Energy Program was introduced by the government of Pierre Trudeau, former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s father.

The policy used price controls, taxes and ownership rules to keep Canadian energy affordable while directing more of Alberta’s revenues to Ottawa.

It has since become a central symbol of “Western alienation”, a term used to describe the sense of disenfranchisement felt among Canada’s westernmost provinces.

Those tensions resurfaced decades later under Justin Trudeau, whose term began in 2015. His climate policies, including a national carbon tax and a limit on emissions, angered Alberta’s oil sector.

“We’ve been fighting about the same things for 50 years,” said Morgan.

Then came the COVID-19 pandemic. Experts say demonstrations against health restrictions mobilised a new generation of conservative activists, breathing new life into Alberta’s separatist movement.

Trudeau ultimately resigned as Liberal Party leader and prime minister in 2025, amid sinking poll numbers. Carney was elected his replacement.

Last year, under growing pressure from separatist groups, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government made it easier to start referendums, helping bring the question of Alberta’s independence onto the political agenda.

For Wesley, the moment is less about growing public support for independence and more about pressure from within Smith’s governing United Conservative Party, whose members show higher support for separation than Albertans generally.

“We’re having a referendum because Danielle Smith wants us to have a referendum,” Wesley said. “She is looking to solve internal party matters by throwing a question to the broader public.”

Though she called Monday’s referendum, Smith has said she opposes the independence effort, and on October 14, she announced she had voted against seceding.

“In my view, now is not the time to give up hope in our country, not when we have fought so long and come so far,” Smith said in a social media video, explaining her vote.

Could defeat make the movement stronger?

Smith’s political gamble has drawn comparisons with the 2016 Brexit referendum in the United Kingdom, including from Carney.

At the time, then-UK Prime Minister David Cameron called a vote over whether the country should leave the European Union, in hopes of settling a debate dividing his own Conservative Party.

Voters ultimately chose to leave the bloc, triggering years of political unrest.

But Ian Cooper, a political scientist who grew up in Alberta and now lives in Ireland, says a more useful comparison might be a different UK referendum in 1975, when British voters chose overwhelmingly to stay in what was then known as the European Economic Community.

That vote, he said, did little to deter those who wanted the country out.

“The activists who were in favour of Brexit — this is before anybody called it Brexit — they really played the long game,” he said. “It took them 25 years, but they finally achieved it.”

Cooper suspects that, even if Alberta separation is roundly defeated, separatists could take a similar approach, pursuing the issue over the long term to gain prominence and support.

“My impression is that they really are true believers, and it’s really ideologically driven,” he said.

If Monday’s separatist vote fails, Morgan said separatists would need to take a hard look at why they had fallen short and work towards making a stronger case for independence in the future.

He does not believe the underlying grievances can be resolved by working within the Canadian system or by electing a more sympathetic federal government.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, acknowledged at Thursday’s rally that “the frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real”. He added that Ottawa had made people in the province feel “like our resources weren’t our own”.

The prime minister has tried, amid an ongoing trade war with the United States, to improve relations with Alberta, including through commitments to building a new pipeline to Canada’s west coast and major infrastructure projects.

Morgan admits that, for those whose goal is simply to get more leverage in Ottawa, “it’s pretty clear the movement has been effective”.

“We’ve seen more love from a federal prime minister in the last year than we’ve seen in the last 10,” Morgan said. “The problem though, when it comes to stubborn independence folks like me, is nothing has changed in the system.”

Prime ministers come and go, he added. “We’re just one election away from another hostile one.”

Why the other referendum questions matter

But the referendum could also offer an opportunity to challenge the premise that Alberta’s grievances cannot be addressed within Canada.

The independence question is just one of 10 on Monday’s ballot. Other proposals include restricting temporary residents’ access to healthcare and education, as well as allowing Alberta to choose its own judges.

Smith has encouraged Albertans to vote in favour of the nine other proposals, arguing that they will give her more negotiating power in Ottawa.

“Many Albertans I speak with tell me they want to send Ottawa a message, and I would suggest the best way to do that is to give us a strong mandate on the other nine questions,” she said on social media.

If Albertans back those proposals but Ottawa refuses to make concessions, Cooper, the political scientist, said the movement would have fresh ammunition to argue that meaningful change within the current system is impossible.

“Buried in the nine other questions are the seeds for a future referendum,” Cooper added.

Not everyone agrees, however, on whether the separatists can emerge from the vote as a united force.

Wesley explained that people have been drawn to the separatist cause for a variety of reasons.

If there’s a sense that independence is not a realistic prospect, there may be little to keep that group of activists together, he said. They could turn their attention to other conservative issues, such as immigration.

Other experts question whether Alberta’s separatist movement, which is united more by economic grievances than by a shared cultural identity, can endure the way Quebec’s has.

Just two weeks ago, the largely French-speaking province elected the separatist Party Quebecois, which has promised a third referendum on independence after Trump leaves office.

Morgan, however, argues that Alberta does have a distinct culture, shaped by generations of people who have moved to the province in search of prosperity.

“The type of person drawn to do that is often an individualistic type of person,” he said. “They want the opportunity to go out and succeed or fail on their own.”

“And that builds a kind of a distinct culture on its own, even if it’s not a long-built one, as you would see in a distinct area like Quebec with a linguistic difference or in another country.”

Even if Albertans reject separation, he believes the movement has succeeded in forcing Ottawa to take the province’s frustrations more seriously.

“Hopefully some people understand that eventually something has to give,” he said. “So whatever the results are … I do hope, at the very least, they’ve served as a wake-up call to a lot of people.”

articles.title: A former meatpacking warehouse sat vacant for years in California before a $6.27 million transformation created a food hub and 51 jobs
articles.summary: A vacant industrial building in Fresno, California, spent years with little apparent purpose beyond occupying a patch of land.
articles.body: A vacant industrial building in Fresno, California, spent years with little apparent purpose beyond occupying a patch of land. It had served different businesses over its lifetime, including a bakery, a petrol station and a meatpacking operation, but its later years brought a different set of problems. Contamination and the deteriorating condition of the structure made the site difficult to reuse. Turning it into something useful required more than renovating the building. Environmental assessments, cleanup planning and a complicated funding effort had to come first. In May 2024, the former warehouse reopened as the Saint Rest + Food to Share Hub, a 6,800-square-foot centre for food distribution, nutrition education and community activities. Its history as a bakery, petrol station and meatpacking plant reflected the changing nature of the site, but by the time redevelopment became a serious possibility, the building presented practical obstacles. articles.title: Macklemore's 'Free Palestine' tour funding anti-Israel org who cheered Oct 7 Hamas attack
articles.summary: Macklemore's "Free Palestine" tour will fund the Palestinian Youth Movement, an organization that was accused of celebrating the Oct. 7 terror attacks.
articles.body: Macklemore's upcoming "Free Palestine" tour later this month will help fund an organization that celebrated the deadly Oct. 7 terror attacks. After the 43-year-old rapper was dropped from Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour" after he repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind’s Hall" last month, Macklemore announced that he would be launching his "Free Palestine" tour in retaliation. The tour includes three shows in Dublin on Oct. 26, in Paris on Oct. 29 and in London on Oct. 30, respectively. According to the tour's website, all proceeds will go to one of twelve organizations, including the Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM), whose leadership has come under fire for several controversial statements. 'SNL' HOST MICHAEL CHE MOCKS MACKLEMORE'S 'FREE PALESTINE TOUR' AFTER ED SHEERAN DROPS RAPPER The Jewish News Syndicate reported that the PYM's U.K. chapter has been accused of defending Hamas' actions during the terror attack three years ago that led to approximately 1,200 casualties and 251 civilians being taken hostage. The organization reportedly referred to these actions as "legitimate" and "effective." Just days after the original attack, a female speaker from the Palestinian Youth Movement was heard cheering the Hamas attacks and terrorists during a protest outside the Israeli consulate in New York. "Thank you…for raising your voices to celebrate the glorious victory of the resistance. And to honor our martyrs and [we're] marching to show those here in the heart of the empire that they will never defeat our struggle. They have failed to break the unity of our people, and they have failed to dampen the revolutionary spirit of our people who grow stronger every day," the woman said. MIKE HUCKABEE CALLS OUT MACKLEMORE ON ANTISEMITISM: 'VOICE' OF 'JEW HATRED' Fox News Digital reached out to Macklemore's representatives and the PYM for comment. In a comment to Fox News Digital, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC), a U.K.-based Jewish organization, called for better efforts to vet Macklemore's charitable organizations and protect Jewish citizens. "When the Palestinian Youth Movement praises young people joining armed factions and describes the 7 October massacre as a ‘prison break’, it risks legitimising violence against Jews. At a time of grave violence and threats against Jewish communities, Live Nation must show how it will protect Jewish audiences and staff from antisemitic incitement and harassment," the JLC said. LIBERAL LAWMAKERS, ACTIVISTS RALLY BEHIND MACKLEMORE AFTER SHEERAN TOUR REMOVAL OVER 'FREE PALESTINE' STANCE It continued, "PYM’s inclusion as a beneficiary of Macklemore’s concert raises serious questions about Live Nation’s vetting of the organisations it helps fund. We need a clear account of the checks undertaken, who will ultimately receive the proceeds and what safeguards will prevent the money being used to fund conduct that threatens the safety of Jews in this country." Fox News Digital reached out to Live Nation for comment but did not immediately receive a reply. The Israeli-American Council, which demanded Macklemore be removed from Sheeran's tour last month, said his recent actions "reinforce the concerns that led the IAC to launch its petition." "Our objection was never to his right to support Palestinians," the group said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "It was to the normalization of antisemitic rhetoric that disregards the suffering and humanity of Jews and Israelis." "Robert Kraft and his fellow stadium owners showed admirable moral leadership when they refused to give Macklemore a platform to voice his message of discrimination and antisemitism. Live Nation and the concert organizers must now publicly explain their vetting process and ensure that concert proceeds do not benefit organizations that justify violence against innocent civilians. Our message to them remains: ‘Your show, your stage, your responsibility,’" the statement continued. In addition to the tour, Macklemore announced on Instagram last month that he would be donating the $1 million he earned as part of Sheeran's tour to six organizations, including Palestine Children's Relief Fund (PCRF), HEAL Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA National Committee and American Near East Refugee Aid (ANERA). articles.title: Trump’s approval rating slips again, and a deadly incident at a youth soccer game: Weekend Rundown
articles.summary: Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.”
articles.body: Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterms, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey. Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions. The president’s approval rating slipped to 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low in this poll, while his disapproval rating rose to 66%. Americans continue to hold a negative view of Democrats, too. Among adults, just 43% view the Democratic Party favorably. Boy and man killed, 10 injured after woman drives through youth soccer game in Kansas A 6-year-old boy and 35-year-old man were killed and 10 others were injured when a woman drove a truck through a youth soccer game at a city sports complex in Wichita, Kansas, Saturday afternoon, police said. The 34-year-old driver was in custody, though it wasn’t immediately clear whether the incident at the Stryker Sports Complex was intentional, police said. “She has been cooperative up to this point in the investigation,” Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said at an evening news conference. There were two children in the truck, Moses said. One of the women’s children had a game at the complex, though at a different field. The injured include five children, ranging in age from 5 to 9 years old, as well as five men and women between 28 and 68 years old, he said. ‘Meet the Press’: Zelenskyy warns U.S. against ‘historic mistake’ Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S. formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake,” but said he still sees Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill. “We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.” Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress. The move came days after U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” Zelenskyy said, leaving Ukraine blind to incoming ballistic missiles. Limits have also been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercepting jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe SpaceX imposed the Starlink limits in response to a “message from American government.” Amid escalating tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dodged three times when asked whether Ukraine is an ally of the United States. “We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” Bessent told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the second time he was asked whether the U.S. considers Ukraine an ally. (Earlier, Bessent said U.S. support includes providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing NATO to purchase U.S. weapons to resell to Ukraine.) Asked for a third time, the treasury secretary simply said, “I’m not the secretary of state. I’m not the president.” Notable quote Zelenskyy responded to Trump suspending new sanctions against Russia that Congress had passed. Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. Politics in brief ‘No Kings’: Rallies opposing Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.D.C. makeover: Trump announced plans to redevelop the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C., which has been at the center of a legal battle over his renovation push.Foreign endorsement: Trump endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the longtime Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election. Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with his surgeon saying he could make a full recovery within about 10 days. Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News there were “no clinical reasons” why the pontiff should not make his planned trip to Latin America next month. Leo, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided and spent a couple minutes speaking to well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling figure of the pope before getting into a car to return to the Vatican. He thanked well-wishers on Sunday as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace. ‘The house was toast’: Surf swallows California homes The worst of El Niño is still months away, but Southern California’s fragile coastline is already being transformed by record-setting king tides and storm surges. An unusually active hurricane season triggered a trio of storms that pummeled Hawaii and Mexico earlier this year. The historic weather pattern claimed more than a dozen homes along the shore in Long Beach, swallowing up boardwalks and portions of the Pacific Coast Highway farther south. “This is just a little bit of a taste of what we will see in the future,” warned Timu Gallien with the Coastal Flood Lab at the University of California, Los Angeles. Golden State Valkyries take Game 1 of WNBA Finals over Atlanta Dream In front of a sold-out sea of purple at the Chase Center, the Golden State Valkyries shook off an early deficit and shooting struggles to beat the Atlanta Dream 68-64 and take Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. Valkyries star Gabby Williams led all scorers with 26 points on 8-of-22 shooting. She hit two free throws with 4.1 seconds remaining to ice the game. Allisha Gray led the Dream with 19 points on 5-of-19 shooting but was held scoreless in the fourth quarter. The Valkyries forced 12 Atlanta turnovers and scored 17 points off of them. Golden State center Kiah Stokes recorded four blocks in the first half to add to the team’s total of 10. More sports news Boxing champion Daniel Dubois retained his WBO heavyweight title with a brutal second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley on Saturday at the O2 Arena in London. In case you missed it Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during demonstrations over rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.Canada’s defense minister said four people were killed and multiple were injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire.A man died after being shot during a dispute at a subway station in Manhattan’s Theater District, according to police.Val Chmerkovskiy received a one-week suspension on “Dancing with the Stars” after a comment he made on social media.A 71-year-old man died after an alligator attacked him while he was fishing, authorities said.

articles.title: Priest in Ecuador dies after crucifix falls on him during livestreamed Mass
articles.summary: The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari was the parish priest at the Church of Perpetual Relief in Guayaquil.
articles.body: A priest in Ecuador died Saturday after a crucifix fell on him during a livestreamed Mass, according to church officials and video of the incident. The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died Saturday, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced. He was the parish priest at the Church of Perpetual Relief of the Central Vicariate, the archdiocese said. Molinari “has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory,” it said in a news release. The Mass was livestreamed, but the video was taken down. The video, reviewed by NBC News, showed a large crucifix hanging on a wall behind Molinari suddenly falling forward onto the back of his head. Molinari was behind the altar, facing the congregation, and did not see the crucifix falling behind him. Molinari did not stand back up, and parishioners are heard on the video shrieking and crying. Some rush to tend to him. A Eucharist in his memory is scheduled for Sunday evening.

articles.title: Shafali Verma scripts history with ninth 50-plus score as India thrash Zimbabwe to seal T20I series
articles.summary: Shafali Verma's explosive 25-ball 55 propelled India to a dominant nine-wicket victory over Zimbabwe in the second T20I, securing a 2-0 lead in the series. T...
articles.body:
Shafali Verma continued her prolific run in women's T20 internationals, smashing a 25-ball 55 as India thrashed Zimbabwe by nine wickets in the second T20I to take an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series on Sunday. The Indian opener set a new benchmark for the most 50-plus scores by a batter in a calendar year in women's T20Is, registering her ninth such innings in 2026. She moved past Smriti Mandhana, who recorded eight 50-plus scores in 2024, while Mithali Raj and Hong Kong's Natasha Miles have seven and eight, respectively, in 2018 and 2026. Shafali's latest half-century, her 22nd in T20Is, came as India chased down Zimbabwe's modest target of 103 in just 8.5 overs after restricting the visitors to 102/8.

Shafali-Mandhana partnership adds to record year

Shafali and captain Smriti Mandhana combined to make short work of the chase, sharing a 96-run opening partnership that put India firmly in control. Mandhana remained unbeaten on 47, while Shafali's aggressive knock featured sixes and boundaries that left Zimbabwe's bowlers struggling for answers. The stand also extended the pair's remarkable record in 2026. Shafali and Mandhana have now registered nine 50-plus partnerships in women's T20Is this calendar year, the most by any pair. They surpassed their own tally of seven such stands in 2024 and moved ahead of Hong Kong's Yasmin Daswani and Natasha Miles, who have eight in 2026.

Most 50-plus stands in a calendar year in Women's T20Is (any wicket)

9 - Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma (IND-W) in 2026

8 - Yasmin Daswani, Natasha Miles (HKG-W) in 2026

7 - Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma (IND-W) in 2024

Shafali reached her half-century in 26 balls, taking on off-spinner Beloved Biza for a six. She also punished Michelle Mavunga with three consecutive deliveries yielding four, four and six. Mandhana, meanwhile, struck four successive boundaries against pacer Nyasha Gwanzura before finishing the chase with an inside-out six off Olinder Chare. The victory also gave Mandhana a series win at the start of her full-time captaincy stint.

India's bowlers restrict Zimbabwe to 102/8

Earlier, India's bowlers delivered a disciplined performance to prevent Zimbabwe from building momentum after the visitors opted to bat first. Nandani Sharma dismissed opener Kelis Ndhlovu for a duck, and Zimbabwe managed only 20 runs in the powerplay. Beloved Biza departed soon after, leaving the visitors under pressure. Chipo Tiripano top-scored with 34 off 32 balls, while captain Josephine Nkomo remained unbeaten on 27. The pair added 45 runs for the fourth wicket, providing Zimbabwe with their most productive phase of the innings. However, off-spinner Niki Prasad broke the stand by having Tiripano caught behind by wicketkeeper Richa Ghosh. Prasad later trapped Nyasha Gwanzura leg-before to finish with figures of 2/7 and leave Zimbabwe restricted to 102/8. India's commanding chase, powered by Shafali's record-setting half-century and her prolific partnership with Mandhana, ensured the hosts secured the series with one match remaining.

articles.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
articles.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment", and saying the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

Trump also claimed in his Truth Social post that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Since then, Zelensky declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing a European Union summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin.

articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has vowed strict action against those involved in rioting and looting across the country, declaring that anyone who
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron has vowed strict action against those involved in rioting and looting across the country, declaring that anyone who sought to undermine the Republic would be held accountable. His remarks came after nationwide protests against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services descended into some of France's worst unrest in recent years, leaving two people dead and hundreds injured.Addressing the nation on Sunday evening, Macron said the violence had left the country feeling both “anger and shame”, as authorities reported around 2,400 arrests following clashes between protesters and police. Masked groups set fire to buildings, attacked public infrastructure and looted businesses in several cities, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges. More than 600 police officers were reportedly injured, while a police officer and a protester died in separate incidents linked to the unrest.The president blamed what he described as radical far-left groups and criminal elements for the destruction, while stressing that the legitimate grievances of peaceful demonstrators should not be confused with acts of violence. The protests, which drew an estimated 550,000 people according to authorities, were organised amid growing anger over fuel prices, living costs and deteriorating public services, including schools.'Those who destroyed must pay': Macron warns rioters“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said in his televised address. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”Condemning what he called “unrestrained violence”, the president described the perpetrators as “seditious elements from far-left factions, joined by numerous delinquents”.“Watching these images, we were all wondering: what had got into them? How can French people do that to France?” he said, adding that “nothing can justify it, explain it or excuse it”.Macron also called for calm and order as disturbances continued on a smaller scale on Sunday. Police fired tear gas and stun grenades at groups gathered at Paris' Place de la République, where protesters had assembled following calls on social media to continue the movement. Clashes and attempts to set fire to bicycles and rubbish bins were also reported.The destruction was particularly severe in Limoges, where flames engulfed the 19th-century town hall on Saturday, causing its roof and clock tower to collapse. In Marseille, masked protesters forced their way into the city hall's lobby, while a fire broke out at a tourist office in Lyon. Hundreds of businesses were also reportedly looted across the country.A 22-year-old police officer died in Nantes after being struck by a vehicle, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Separately, a protester died following a cardiorespiratory arrest near Paris, with authorities investigating the circumstances.Government to engage protesters as political tensions riseDespite his condemnation of the violence, Macron insisted that the government must acknowledge the concerns driving the demonstrations.“Yesterday, hundreds of thousands of our compatriots demonstrated to state legitimate claims,” he said. “Never must we confuse the latter with those who destroyed and vandalized.”He said he had asked the government to bring together students, teachers, trade unionists and other stakeholders this week to discuss concrete proposals addressing their concerns. Macron also instructed regional prefects to coordinate with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses, including through protest bans where necessary.The unrest has also intensified political divisions ahead of France's next presidential election. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen criticised Macron's government as exhausted and incapable of responding effectively, while left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of escalating tensions through his handling of the situation.Mélenchon, who joined Saturday's march in Paris, nevertheless rejected looting and destruction, saying those who shared the movement's objectives had no place engaging in such acts.You use AI every day.
